title: Who Does America Owe $40 Trillion To?

youtube.title: Who Does America Owe $40 Trillion To? (Not China)
youtube.hook: America owes $40 trillion. Most people think China owns America. China holds less than 2%. So who are the real lenders? The biggest one might surprise you: it's America itself. Here's the national debt, explained simply.

sources: U.S. Treasury, Debt to the Penny (Sept 21, 2026): total public debt $40.11T; debt held by the public $32.40T; intragovernmental holdings $7.71T
U.S. Treasury, Treasury International Capital data for July 2026: foreign holdings $9.16T; Japan $1.15T; United Kingdom $899.3B; China $730.7B (lowest since 2009)
Federal Reserve H.4.1 (Sept 2026): Treasury securities held ≈ $4.56T
CBO: debt held by the public ≈ 100% of GDP (FY2025)
Moody's downgraded the U.S. credit rating from Aaa to Aa1 in May 2025
U.S. Census Bureau population estimate ≈ 343 million (2026); $40.1T ÷ 343M ≈ $117,000 per person
Stack math: $100 bill thickness ≈ 0.11 mm; $40.1T in $100 bills ≈ 44,000 km, more than Earth's circumference (≈ 40,075 km)

beats.text: America owes forty trillion dollars.
That's about one hundred and seventeen thousand dollars for every single person in the country. Including babies.
So who did America borrow all that money from?
Most people say: China. China owns America.
Nope. China holds less than two percent of it.
The biggest lender to America is a lot closer than you think. In fact, you might be one of them. Let's find out.
First, where does the debt come from?
Remember our last video? Almost every year, the government spends more than it collects in taxes. That gap is the deficit.
To fill the gap, it borrows. And every year's borrowing gets added to the pile. That pile is the national debt.
How does the government borrow? It sells IOUs called Treasury bonds. You give the government money today, it promises to pay you back later, with interest.
Now, forty trillion dollars is hard to imagine. So let's try.
If you stacked forty trillion dollars in one hundred dollar bills, the stack would be so long, it could wrap all the way around the Earth. And then some.
Now, let's meet the lenders. Starting with the famous one. China.
China holds about seven hundred thirty billion dollars of American debt.
That sounds huge. But out of forty trillion, it's less than two percent. And it's the lowest amount China has held since two thousand nine.
In fact, China isn't even the biggest foreign lender. Japan is, with about one point one five trillion.
Then the United Kingdom, with about nine hundred billion.
Add up every foreign country in the world, and they hold about nine point two trillion. Roughly one quarter.
So if foreigners own one quarter... who owns the other three quarters?
Here's the plot twist. America mostly owes... America.
Lender number one: the government itself. About seven point seven trillion dollars.
Wait. How can you owe yourself money?
Remember the Social Security tax on Dave's paycheck? For many years, workers paid in more than retirees took out. The extra was saved in a trust fund.
And that fund was lent to the Treasury. So one part of the government holds IOUs from another part. It's like Dave's left pocket lending money to his right pocket.
Lender number two: the Federal Reserve. America's central bank holds about four and a half trillion dollars of government bonds.
Remember our first video? Banks create money with a click. Well, the Federal Reserve can do that too. That's how it bought many of these bonds.
And lender number three, the biggest group of all: American investors.
Banks. Pension funds. Insurance companies. Money market funds. State governments. And regular people.
If you have a retirement account, a money market fund, or even an old savings bond from grandma, you might own a tiny piece of America's debt.
So, in a strange way, many Americans are both the borrower and the lender.
But why would anyone lend to a government that's already forty trillion dollars in debt?
Because Treasury bonds are considered one of the safest investments on the planet.
The US government has the power to tax the biggest economy in the world. And it borrows in its own currency, the dollar.
And the dollar is the world's favorite money. Countries use it to trade oil, to hold savings, to feel safe.
So when the world gets scared, money often runs toward American bonds, not away from them.
So is forty trillion dollars a problem? Here's the honest answer. It depends on how you look at it.
The good news: a country is not a household. It doesn't retire. It doesn't die. It can keep rolling its debt forward, paying old bonds with new bonds.
The worrying news: the interest bill is exploding. Remember? About nine hundred seventy billion dollars last year. More than the military.
The debt held by investors is now about the same size as the entire American economy.
And in twenty twenty five, Moody's, one of the big credit rating agencies, lowered America's rating from its perfect top score.
It's like a report card. Still a very good grade. But no longer perfect.
So here's the question everyone asks. Why doesn't America just print forty trillion dollars and pay it all off?
Let's go back to the duck.
Imagine a town with a hundred loaves of bread, and a hundred dollars. Each loaf costs about one dollar.
Now the town prints another hundred dollars. But there's still only one hundred loaves.
More money chasing the same bread. So what happens to the price? It goes up.
That's called inflation. Print too much money, and everyone's money buys less.
Countries have tried it. In two thousand eight, Zimbabwe printed so much money that prices were doubling in about a day. People carried cash in wheelbarrows.
Printing money doesn't make the debt disappear. It just moves the pain to everyone's wallet.
So let's recap.
One. America owes about forty trillion dollars. China holds less than two percent.
Two. Most of the debt is owed to Americans. The government's own trust funds, the Federal Reserve, banks, pension funds, and regular people.
Three. You can't just print your way out. That leads to inflation.
And inflation is happening right now, in your wallet. Slowly. Quietly.
Nobody touched your hundred dollar bill. But it buys less every year. Why?
That's next. Subscribe, before your money shrinks any further.
